core: Observational learning: acquiring behavior patterns by watching a model, without performing them and without reinforcement to the observer
Bandura's four subprocesses of observational learning: attentional, retention, production (originally motor reproduction), and motivational processes
Vicarious reinforcement and vicarious punishment, and the acquisition-versus-performance distinction they support
The Bobo doll studies: the 1961 live-model design and the 1963 film-mediated design, and what each did and did not demonstrate
Reciprocal determinism / triadic reciprocal causation among personal factors, behavior, and environment
Why Bandura relabelled social learning theory as social cognitive theory (1986)

Self-efficacy, its definition as a domain-specific capability judgment, and its four sources: mastery experience, vicarious experience, social/verbal persuasion, and physiological and affective states
Classroom applications: teacher modeling of thinking, worked examples, peer and coping models, and efficacy-building feedback
Honest statement of the media-effects dispute as unresolved rather than settled in either direction
supporting: Model-observer similarity and its effect on vicarious experience
Coping models versus mastery models; multiple models
The inhibitory effect of nonaggressive models observed in the 1961 study
Collective efficacy as an extension of the construct
outOfScope: Detailed treatment of reinforcement schedules, the four operant contingencies, and classical conditioning (covered in education:learning-theories:behaviorism)
Self-regulated learning as a full topic
Media regulation, ratings policy, and First Amendment doctrine beyond one factual reference to how the evidence has been read
Clinical or therapeutic applications of modeling, including guided mastery treatment for phobias
Individualized advice about a specific child's aggression or screen use

claims.claim: In the 1961 experiment, 72 children (36 boys, 36 girls) aged 37-69 months (mean 52 months) from the Stanford University Nursery School were assigned in equal groups of 24 to an aggressive-model, nonaggressive-model, or control condition, with model sex and subject sex counterbalanced within the model conditions.
In the 1961 experiment every child, including controls, was mildly frustrated before testing by being shown attractive toys and then told the toys were reserved for other children.

Children who observed the aggressive model reproduced the model's distinctive physical and verbal aggressive acts significantly more than children in the nonaggressive-model and control groups; roughly 70% of nonaggressive-model and control children scored zero on the imitative measures. Boys produced more imitative physical aggression than girls, and the male model exerted greater overall influence.

The 1961 study also found an inhibitory effect: children who observed the nonaggressive model, particularly the male nonaggressive model, showed significantly less aggression than the no-model controls on several measures.

The authors of the 1961 study explicitly cautioned that comparing subgroups when overall tests do not reach significance risks capitalizing on chance, and that their assumption that model sex rather than some other model characteristic was the operative variable could not be tested with their data.

The 1963 follow-up, 'Imitation of film-mediated aggressive models', compared a live adult model, a filmed human model, and a filmed cartoon model against a control condition; children who viewed the aggressive human and cartoon models on film exhibited nearly twice as much aggression as control children.

Bandura describes observational learning as governed by four component subfunctions: attentional processes, retention processes, motor reproduction (later termed production) processes, and motivational processes.

Vicarious reinforcement occurs when observers see a model reinforced and increase their own production of the behavior; vicarious punishment reduces the observer's motivation to perform it. Bandura distinguished acquisition from performance because people do not perform everything they learn, and identified direct, vicarious, and self-produced incentives.

Reciprocal determinism is the view that personal factors (cognition, affect, and biological events), behavior, and environmental influences interact bidirectionally in a triadic reciprocality, so people are producers as well as products of their environments.

Bandura changed the label of his theory from social learning to social cognitive, with the 1986 publication of Social Foundations of Thought and Action: A Social Cognitive Theory, both to distance it from the prevalent social learning theories of the day (including Miller and Dollard's 1941 account) and to emphasize the critical role of cognition in constructing reality, self-regulating, encoding information, and performing behaviors.

Self-efficacy beliefs are people's judgments of their capabilities to organize and execute the courses of action required to attain designated types of performances; they are judgments of capability rather than of self-worth, and they are distinct from outcome expectations, which are judgments about the consequences a behavior will produce.

Self-efficacy is formed by interpreting information from four sources: mastery experience, vicarious experience, social (verbal) persuasion, and physiological and affective states. Mastery experience is generally the most influential source because it is the most authentic indicator of capability; vicarious experience is weaker but matters more when the observer is uncertain or inexperienced and perceives the model as similar; social persuasion is not the same as knee-jerk praise and works only when the success it envisions is attainable.

In a longitudinal study of preservice teachers, mastery experiences significantly predicted changes in teacher self-efficacy in both a beginning and an advanced practicum group, with the other sources acting largely indirectly through how mastery experiences were interpreted.

Peer models can raise observers' self-efficacy and skill more than a teacher model or no model; peer coping models, who make errors, verbalize coping statements, and gradually succeed, produce higher self-efficacy and performance than peer mastery models, especially when learners have little task familiarity or a history of difficulty, and multiple models perform as well as a single coping model.

The IES practice guide Organizing Instruction and Study to Improve Student Learning (2007) recommends interleaving worked example solutions with problem-solving exercises, at a moderate level of evidence.

The IES/WWC practice guide Teaching Secondary Students to Write Effectively (2016) gives its Recommendation 1, to explicitly teach appropriate writing strategies using a Model-Practice-Reflect instructional cycle, a rating of strong evidence.

The APA's 2020 revision of its resolution on violent video games states that scientific research has demonstrated an association between violent video game use and increases in aggressive behavior, affect, and cognition and decreases in prosocial behavior, empathy, and moral engagement; that reported meta-analytic effect sizes (0.19, 0.15, 0.08, 0.16) have been interpreted dramatically differently; that insufficient research has examined whether violent video game use causes lethal violence; and that the resolution should not be misused by attributing violence such as mass shootings to violent video game use.

In Brown v. Entertainment Merchants Association, 564 U.S. 786 (2011), the U.S. Supreme Court majority endorsed a lower court's assessment that the psychological literature on violent video games is nearly all correlational rather than causal and that most studies carry admitted methodological flaws, and it described the demonstrated effects as small and not specific to video games.

The Bobo doll experiments have been criticized on methodological and interpretive grounds, including the artificiality of the laboratory setting, separation from parents and unfamiliar adults and rooms, the deliberate frustration procedure, the availability of alternative explanations for the children's behavior, and the ethics of exposing children to modelled violence.

Meta-analytic work reports a positive association between academic self-efficacy and academic performance, with evidence that the two are related reciprocally over time rather than in one direction only.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether exposure to violent media causes real-world violence
positions: APA's 2020 resolution: a reliable association exists between violent video game use and aggressive behavior, affect, and cognition, and reduced prosocial behavior, empathy, and moral engagement, replicated across methods and samples.

APA's own resolution: reported meta-analytic effect sizes are small (0.08-0.19) and have been interpreted dramatically differently by the researchers who produced them; insufficient research has examined lethal violence; the resolution explicitly warns against attributing events such as mass shootings to game use.

The Supreme Court majority in Brown v. Entertainment Merchants Association read the literature as correlational, methodologically flawed, and showing effects too small and too unspecific to support restriction.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports the dispute rather than resolving it. It states what the Bobo studies demonstrated (imitation of specific modelled acts under specific laboratory conditions), separates that from the media-effects question, and presents the association-versus-causation gap and the small, contested effect sizes as the current state of the argument.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Direction of the self-efficacy and achievement relationship
positions: Self-efficacy beliefs influence effort, persistence, and subsequent performance.
Prior performance is itself the main input to self-efficacy, so much of the observed correlation runs from achievement to belief.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both are stated. The lesson treats the relationship as reciprocal and warns that raising stated confidence without producing genuine mastery experience is not supported.

positions: Bandura's 1977 social learning formulation calls it motor reproduction.
Later social cognitive formulations call it production, which covers non-motor performances.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson gives both terms and explains that the change tracks the theory's widening beyond motor acts.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained no substantive claims about Bandura, modeling, self-efficacy, or the Bobo doll studies; its body text was subject-agnostic boilerplate ('Social Learning Theory is a foundational concept in Education') and was discarded entirely.
The draft's vocabulary list defined social learning theory as 'a foundational Education concept covered in this lesson', which is circular and carries no content.
The draft's three quick-check questions tested generic study advice rather than the theory and were replaced.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the boilerplate definition with observational learning, the four subprocesses, vicarious consequences, reciprocal determinism, and self-efficacy.

Added accurate 1961 and 1963 Bobo doll designs from the primary 1961 article and a source-verified account of the 1963 follow-up, including the frustration procedure and the inhibitory effect the popular summaries omit.
Added an explicit statement of what the Bobo studies did not show, with the APA resolution's own cautions and effect sizes and the Supreme Court's contrary reading of the same literature.
Added Bandura's stated reasons for the 1986 relabelling to social cognitive theory.

Kept reinforcement terminology consistent with the behaviorism lesson (reinforcement raises the future likelihood of a behavior; punishment lowers it) and deliberately did not re-teach the four operant contingencies.
Used Bandura's own subprocess terms and flagged the motor reproduction / production naming change rather than presenting a single modern label as original.
rightsIssues: The 1961 article is reproduced by Classics in the History of Psychology (York University) but remains under journal copyright; recorded REFERENCE_ONLY and no wording reproduced.
OpenStax terms were not separately verified for this project per the subject source-map caution; recorded REFERENCE_ONLY with no license asserted.

The Pajares overview is a scholarly summary hosted on a university faculty page with no stated reuse license; recorded REFERENCE_ONLY and used only for verified facts, with all prose written independently.
Frontiers articles (Pfitzner-Eden 2016; Galanaki and Malafantis 2022; Yokoyama 2019) carry CC BY 4.0 and are attributed, though no wording was adapted from them either.
The Brown v. Entertainment Merchants Association opinion is a U.S. federal court work in the public domain; the text was checked on a Cornell LII mirror.

sourceRecords.title: Transmission of Aggression Through Imitation of Aggressive Models (Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 63, 575-582)
sourceRecords.provider: Albert Bandura, Dorothea Ross and Sheila A. Ross; reproduced by Classics in the History of Psychology, York University
sourceRecords.notes: Primary source for the 1961 design and results: 72 Stanford University Nursery School children aged 37-69 months (mean 52), three conditions of 24 with model sex counterbalanced, the mild aggression-arousal procedure, the imitative / partially imitative / nonimitative response categories, the sex differences, the inhibitory effect of the nonaggressive model, and the authors' own statistical cautions. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Bandura, Ross, and Ross: Observational Learning and the Bobo Doll (ERIC ED499095)
sourceRecords.provider: Anthony R. Artino, Jr., University of Connecticut; Education Resources Information Center (IES, U.S. Department of Education)
sourceRecords.notes: Scholarly review used for the 1963 film-mediated follow-up (live, filmed human, and cartoon models against a control; exposure groups roughly twice as aggressive as controls, quoting the original at p. 9), for the four component subfunctions as stated in Bandura 1989, for the acquisition-versus-performance distinction and the three types of incentive motivator (direct, vicarious, self-produced), and for the intellectual context of Freudian catharsis and Skinnerian reinforcement that the studies argued against. Reuse terms not stated; used as reference only.

sourceRecords.title: Overview of Social Cognitive Theory and of Self-Efficacy
sourceRecords.provider: Frank Pajares, Emory University (copy hosted by Western Kentucky University)
sourceRecords.notes: Used for the theory's lineage (Miller and Dollard 1941; Bandura and Walters 1963; Bandura 1977; Bandura 1986), Bandura's stated reasons for relabelling the theory social cognitive, the triadic reciprocality formulation of reciprocal determinism, the four observational-learning processes named as attention, retention, production, and motivation, the definition of self-efficacy as judgments of capability to organize and execute courses of action, the efficacy-versus-outcome-expectation distinction, and the four sources of efficacy information including the caution that social persuasion is not knee-jerk praise. No stated reuse license; reference only.

sourceRecords.title: Psychology 2e, Section 6.4: Observational Learning (Modeling)
sourceRecords.notes: Open psychology text used for the standard four-step framing of the modeling process, the three model types (live, verbal instructional, symbolic), and the definitions of vicarious reinforcement and vicarious punishment as changes in the observer's motivation to imitate. Per the subject source-map caution, OpenStax terms were not separately verified for this project; treated as reference only and no license is asserted here.

sourceRecords.title: Why Do I Feel More Confident? Bandura's Sources Predict Preservice Teachers' Latent Changes in Teacher Self-Efficacy (Frontiers in Psychology, 7, 1486)
sourceRecords.license: CC BY 4.0 (stated on the article page)
sourceRecords.notes: Peer-reviewed education study used for the four sources of self-efficacy in Bandura's terms (mastery experiences, vicarious experiences, verbal persuasion, physiological and affective states), for the finding that mastery experiences generally have the strongest effect because they are the most authentic indicators of capability, for the result that mastery experiences predicted change in teacher self-efficacy in both practicum groups while other sources acted largely indirectly, and for the negative association between physiological and affective states and perceived mastery. Facts synthesized; no wording adapted.

sourceRecords.title: Social Origins of Self-Regulatory Competence: The Role of Observational Learning through Peer Modeling (ERIC ED381275)
sourceRecords.provider: Dale H. Schunk and Barry J. Zimmerman; Education Resources Information Center (IES, U.S. Department of Education)
sourceRecords.notes: Review by the principal researchers on modeling in education, used for the definition of modeling as patterning behavior, strategies, thoughts, beliefs, and affects after a model; the comparison of peer mastery models, peer coping models, teacher models, and no model on self-efficacy and skill; the finding that coping models help most when learners lack task familiarity or have a history of difficulty; the equivalence of multiple models to a single coping model; and the role of perceived similarity in judging a model's performance as diagnostic of one's own capability. Reuse terms not stated; reference only.

sourceRecords.title: APA Resolution on Violent Video Games: February 2020 Revision to the 2015 Resolution
sourceRecords.notes: Professional-body policy document used for the current mainstream position and its explicit limits: an association with aggressive behavior, affect, and cognition and with reduced prosocial behavior, empathy, and moral engagement; the four meta-analytic effect sizes (0.19, 0.15, 0.08, 0.16) whose interpretations have varied dramatically; the statement that all violence is aggression but not all aggression is violence and that the literature has not focused on lethal violence; and the opening caution that the resolution should not be misused by attributing violence such as mass shootings to violent video game use. sourceRecords.title: Albert Bandura's experiments on aggression modeling in children: A psychoanalytic critique (Frontiers in Psychology, 13, 988877)
sourceRecords.provider: Evangelia P. Galanaki and Konstantinos D. Malafantis; Frontiers Media
sourceRecords.license: CC BY 4.0 (stated on the article page)
sourceRecords.notes: Peer-reviewed critique used narrowly to establish that substantive methodological, interpretive, and ethical objections to the Bobo doll paradigm exist in the literature: the artificiality of the setting, separation from parents and unfamiliar adults and rooms, the deliberate frustration procedure, the availability of competing explanations for the children's behavior, and the ethics of exposing children to modelled violence. The article's own psychoanalytic alternative is not endorsed in the lesson.

sourceRecords.title: Academic Self-Efficacy and Academic Performance in Online Learning: A Mini Review (Frontiers in Psychology, 9, 2794)
sourceRecords.license: CC BY 4.0 (stated on the article page)
sourceRecords.notes: Peer-reviewed mini review used for the summary of the meta-analytic literature: academic self-efficacy is positively associated with academic performance across a large body of studies (Honicke and Broadbent's 53-study review found only six with no significant correlation), and longitudinal meta-analysis indicates the relationship runs in both directions over time. Used to support the lesson's caution that the correlation does not by itself license a one-way causal claim.
